question_bank.question: In the windowed wake-word labeling scheme, when should a short audio window receive label 1?
choices: When the window begins before any speech activity is detected in the room.
When the window contains only background noise after the trigger phrase.
When the window ends just after the speaker has finished saying the trigger phrase.
When the window contains any spoken word with similar duration to the trigger phrase.
question_bank.explanation: The positive label is aligned to the event completion: a window is positive when the phrase has just finished and the lamp should respond.

source_ref.evidence_span: This is where they just finished saying Robert, turn on.

frame_evidence.description: Whiteboard shows an audio waveform/timeline with vertical marks indicating windows around the spoken phrase.

question_bank.question: Why does sliding a window over each long recording make the initial wake-word dataset easier to train on?
choices: It converts a small set of long clips into many local binary examples aligned to candidate event times.
It converts every negative region into a positive example so the model sees the phrase more often.
It removes the need to know where the trigger phrase occurs in each original recording.
It forces the network to classify complete recordings instead of shorter local segments.
question_bank.explanation: Windowing turns each longer clip into multiple short examples, letting one annotated recording yield many binary training instances.

source_ref.evidence_span: 100 training examples and turn that into 3,000 binary examples.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor stands beside the timeline drawing where multiple adjacent windows are cut from one waveform.

question_bank.question: A wake-word classifier reports high accuracy but produces zero detections. What diagnosis best matches the lecture?
choices: The model has learned a useful trigger detector, but the audio preprocessing hides it at inference time.
The train and dev sets are balanced, but the threshold is too low for positive windows.
The windows are too short to contain the trigger phrase, so positives become mislabeled negatives.
The dataset is skewed, so always predicting the majority negative class can look accurate.
question_bank.explanation: A high headline accuracy is misleading when positives are rare. Predicting zero all the time can score well while failing the actual product goal.

source_ref.evidence_span: all the time that had 0 detections.

frame_evidence.description: Whiteboard lists the window labels while the instructor describes the 97% accurate model that detects nothing.

question_bank.question: What practical imbalance fix does the instructor say can work for the positive wake-word windows?
choices: Drop all background-only windows so the classifier trains only on the trigger phrase.
Merge the positive and negative labels into a single unlabeled audio class.
Replace binary labels with a random label for each window to regularize the model.
Duplicate positive examples so the learner sees them more often during training.
question_bank.explanation: The lecture notes that making multiple copies of positive examples can be a simple and effective tactic for a skewed windowed dataset.

source_ref.evidence_span: your positive examples and just making multiple copies of that

frame_evidence.description: Instructor points at the board near the positive/negative examples while discussing how to rebalance the window labels.

question_bank.question: Why is the 1-to-30 wake-word window ratio riskier than the smaller imbalance ratios the instructor says networks often handle?
choices: It makes positive windows too common, so the model tends to trigger on any speech.
It gives the negative class enough dominance that a naive accuracy metric can hide missed positives.
It makes every three-second clip too short for the phrase to fit inside the window.
It prevents the use of binary labels because the task becomes multi-class by definition.
question_bank.explanation: The instructor contrasts manageable imbalance with the 1-to-30 example, where the majority class can dominate training and metrics.

source_ref.evidence_span: In this example, we have a 1 to 30 ratio.

frame_evidence.description: Whiteboard notes include the positive and negative counts as the instructor explains why the skewed ratio causes failure.
